The state of the store¶

What has been built out of OpenStreetMap so far, what it fixed, what is still open, and what each of those numbers looks like on the ground.

Every number here is read from the live PostGIS store, and every one that also appears in review/README.md is the same query — the metric definitions are imported from export.review_bundle rather than retyped, so the two cannot drift apart. Colours come from the *_class columns the qa.v_* views already carry, which is what QGIS colours by, for the same reason.

The maps sit on tiles — a pale reference map to place things, aerial imagery where the ground itself is the point. They are fetched when the notebook executes and rasterised into the pictures, so this page still opens with no network; only a refresh needs one. Their attribution stays on each map, because those tiles are somebody's work under a licence.

Refresh it with:

cd pipeline
uv run --group notebook jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute \
    --inplace notebooks/state.ipynb
uv run --group notebook jupyter nbconvert --to html \
    notebooks/state.ipynb --output state.html

Two steps, and in that order: the first runs the notebook and keeps its outputs, the second renders those same outputs to HTML. Executing twice would leave the page and the notebook reporting two different runs.

In [1]:
import sys
from pathlib import Path

# This is a non-packaged uv project with flat modules, so `core` and
# `export` only resolve from pipeline/. nbconvert runs with the notebook's
# own directory as cwd, so find the root rather than assuming it.
root = next(p for p in [Path.cwd(), *Path.cwd().parents] if (p / "core.py").exists())
sys.path[:0] = [str(root), str(root / "notebooks")]

1 · What there is¶

The ten numbers the build is measured by. Network length is the integrity check: a pass that moves it has either invented ground or thrown some away, which is why every repair is judged against it staying still.

2 · Where it is¶

The whole routing network in one frame, coloured by steepness, with the two ingested regions boxed and every start drawn as a dot. Lecco and Bergamo are one connected network, not two — which is why a route can cross between them.

In [5]:
network = rd.geoframe(
    """
    SELECT edge_id, steepness_class,
           ST_SimplifyPreserveTopology(geom, 0.0004) AS geom
    FROM qa.v_network
    """
)
starts = rd.geoframe("SELECT vertex_id, geom FROM qa.v_start")
rd.network_map(network, starts)
Out[5]:

3 · How it got here¶

Findings are kept per run, so the repair history is a query rather than a note somebody wrote down. Four rules were driven to zero; islands drift down as coverage widens; overlap is the one that moved the wrong way, and it is the queue that is still open below.

Green means the rule now reports nothing.

In [6]:
rd.history_chart(rd.finding_history())
Out[6]:

4 · What is settled¶

The claims this build has earned. The repairs are the load-bearing one: a detector that finds a defect is worth little unless the fix can be shown not to have moved the ground underneath it.

In [7]:
rd.metrics("settled")[["label", "value", "note"]]
Out[7]:
label value note
0 Every repairable topology defect is at zero 0 findings across the four repairable rules - and the network kept every metre while the...
1 Route relations joined 752 of 752, with 10,361 edges that had no name of their own now carrying one
2 The DEM agrees with the ground 160 saddles checked against their OSM `ele` tag: median error 4.1 m. Judge the DEM on sadd...
3 Every staged source is read by something 7 distinct builders have run over this store - ways, relations, the DEM, POIs, settlemen...
In [8]:
fixes = rd.frame(
    "SELECT fix_id, rule, start_moved_m, end_moved_m FROM qa.v_fix"
)
rd.fix_histogram(fixes)
Out[8]:

The tolerance is not a guess: 2 m came from the near-miss histogram, where 231 of 14,769 loose ends fall inside it and the distribution's own peak sits at 6–8 m — deep inside the real-dead-end population. Nothing crosses the line, so no repair reached past the evidence for it.

Only two of the four repair rules are on that chart, and that is the point. gap_dangle_pair and gap_dangle_junction MOVE an endpoint, so the tolerance binds them. The other two do not move anything: gap_dangle_edge splits an edge at a point and degenerate collapses a sub-metre one, so their end_moved_m measures the piece that resulted, not a distance the ground travelled. Read together, the four say a repair moved something 555 m — which never happened. The bundle's blanket nothing should have moved more than the 2 m tolerance is true of the snaps and misleading over all four.

5 · What is open, and where¶

Ordered by how much each matters, not by size — a zero here is good news. The scale is logarithmic because they span 12 to 7,170.

In [10]:
overlaps = rd.geoframe(
    "SELECT finding_id, shared_m, geom FROM qa.v_overlap"
)
islands = rd.geoframe(
    "SELECT finding_id, vertices, geom FROM qa.v_island"
)
rd.findings_map(
    network, {"overlaps to judge": overlaps, "islands": islands}
)
Out[10]:

Overlap is the one queue no rule can close: a duplicate, a bridge and two ways legitimately sharing a stretch look identical from the outside. Islands are deliberately not repaired — welding one to the network would invent a connection that is not there.

6 · What a number looks like on the ground¶

A count is a claim about real ground. Six of them, each drawn over the network around it and captioned with the measure that picked it out.

In the repair panel, grey dashed is where the endpoint was and red is where it is. In the urban-exit panel, green is a way out onto trail and grey is the town continuing — the judgement the start rule asks for.

Out[11]:

7 · What has been mapped¶

The 752 route relations that contributors have drawn over this ground, grouped by the area their member edges fall in. 61 run through both, and they are their own group rather than being pushed into whichever region happens to hold more of them.

The colours tell routes apart; they do not name them. 388 share the Lecco panel, so no palette could name them all — what a colour has to do here is let the eye follow one line where several cross, and they cycle through twenty so two that touch are almost never the same. The longest few in each area are named, because those are the ones a walker recognises.

In [12]:
routes = rd.mapped_routes()
rd.mapped_routes_map(routes)
Out[12]:

8 · The same routes, by category¶

The panels above answer where; this answers what. Two questions, and one map cannot carry both without becoming a mess.

Hiking is nearly everything — 684 of 752 relations and 2,855 of the 3,580 km — and it sits where you would expect: the mountains. The bicycle relations run the valleys and the city, and the 25 MTB ones are few but long, holding a corridor of their own along the ridge.

9 · Up close, over the ground itself¶

A reference map says where a line is. Imagery says what it goes through — forest, scree, a lake shore, the edge of a town — which is the question a walker actually has, and the one no categorised colour can answer.

Each route is drawn twice, a wide pale line under a thin dark one: a single stroke over aerial imagery disappears into it.

In [15]:
# The Via Mercatorum over its forested slopes, the Via delle Sorelle
# around Bergamo, and the Ciclovia Gialla along its ridge.
rd.route_closeups(routes, [9752308, 20354969, 15975925])
Out[15]:

10 · One route in full¶

The profile is the thing distance alone cannot tell you: 35 km along a lake and 35 km over a ridge are the same number and not the same day. Beside it, everything a card would carry about the same route.

Getting this right needed the edges in walking order, which is not the order the relation lists them in. Measured on this very route: its member 88 sits at 99.93% along the merged line, so the members run backwards and start two thirds of the way through. Ordered by member index, the profile grew cliffs that are not on the hill; ordered along the line — the same ST_LineLocatePoint the pipeline uses to place a POI on a route — it climbs from 326 m, runs four tops along the ridge, and comes down.

In [16]:
rd.route_profile_card(9752308)
Out[16]:

11 · The catalogue¶

The routes generated from those starts: how long, how much climb, and how much of each stays off the road. Score is descriptive and never a filter — what counts as enough trail is a product decision, not a build step's.

In [17]:
draw = rd.geoframe(
    """
    SELECT route_id, km, ascent_m, off_road_share, score,
           offroad_class, shape_class, mtb_class, geom
    FROM qa.v_draw
    """
)
rd.catalogue_charts(draw)
Out[17]:

Where to look next. The open list above is ordered on purpose: the 164 overlaps are the only queue that needs a person, and the routes matching under 20% of their ways are the ones that would ship a fragment under a famous name. Everything below those is coverage or naming — real, and not in the way.

For judging one geometry at a time, this page is the wrong tool: open review/vaivia-qa.gpkg in QGIS and sort the layer by its measure. This one answers where the build is; that one answers whether a particular line is right.
